opus-5.5.text:
I think data is really the biggest bottleneck in robotics right now. If you look at what happened with large language models, the breakthrough didn't come only from better architectures. It came from scale: trillions of tokens of text that were already sitting on the internet. Robotics doesn't have that. There's no internet-scale corpus of robot actions. Every piece of robot data has to be collected, usually by a human teleoperating a robot, one episode at a time. That's slow and expensive, and it simply doesn't scale the way we need it to.

With Gemini Robotics 1.5, we made good progress on things like reasoning before acting, and motion transfer, where data collected on one robot embodiment helps another. That's an important step, because it means we're no longer starting from zero for every new robot. But it doesn't remove the fundamental problem. The model is still bounded by the amount and diversity of physical interaction data we can feed it.

So when I think about what comes next, I keep coming back to how we can get orders of magnitude more data. A few directions are promising to me. One is learning from human videos. There's an enormous amount of footage of people manipulating objects, cooking, and fixing things. If we can extract useful signal from that despite the embodiment gap, it's a huge resource. Another is simulation, and increasingly world models, where you generate experience instead of collecting it all in the real world. A third is getting robots deployed so they can collect data themselves and improve through their own experience, the way reinforcement learning promises but at real scale.

The reason I think this matters so much is that I believe the scaling laws we've seen in other domains will apply to robotics too. We just haven't been able to reach the regime where they really kick in, because we're data-starved. Whoever figures out a scalable data recipe, one where more compute and more robots translate directly into more useful data and better models, will unlock the next big jump. To me that's more fundamental than any single model improvement. It's the flywheel that makes everything else possible.

r001.rationale: The response identifies scalable alternatives to one-episode-at-a-time teleoperation data: learning from human videos, generating experience in simulation or world models, and collecting data through deployed robots.

r002.rationale: It says scalable data could unlock robotics’ next big jump and make further progress possible, but does not clearly say this could bring solving robotics within reach.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that data is the bottleneck, and it has been the bottleneck for a long time. If you look at why language models and vision models took off, the recipe was fairly simple in hindsight: a scalable architecture, a scalable training objective, and an essentially unlimited supply of data from the internet. Robotics has the first two now. What it doesn't have is the third.

With Gemini Robotics 1.5 we showed that a lot of the generalization you want, the ability to understand a scene, reason about a task, and transfer across different robot bodies, really does come from scale and from leveraging the web knowledge already in Gemini. But the embodied part, the part where the model has to actually output motor commands that work in the physical world, still relies heavily on teleoperation data. And teleoperation is expensive. You need a human, a robot, a physical scene, and real time passing. There's no way to make that ten thousand times cheaper the way crawling another corner of the internet is cheap.

So when I say scalable data is the direction, I mean a few things. One is simulation, which is where I've spent a lot of my career. Simulation gives you parallelism and diversity you can't get physically, and I think the sim-to-real gap is shrinking fast, partly because the models themselves are becoming more robust to visual and dynamic variation. Another is human video. There are billions of hours of humans doing things with their hands, and if we can learn the right representations from that, even without action labels, it changes the economics completely. A third is the robots themselves generating data, running autonomously, trying things, and learning from the outcome, which starts to look like reinforcement learning at scale rather than imitation.

And the reason this matters beyond 1.5 is that I don't think the next big jump comes from a cleverer architecture. It comes from closing the loop between the data engine and the model. If every deployed robot, every simulation run, and every piece of human video can feed back into training, you get the flywheel that made the other fields move so quickly. Without that, we are iterating on model design while being starved of the one thing that has mattered most everywhere else.

r001.rationale: The response identifies teleoperation as expensive and proposes simulation, human video, and autonomous robot experience as scalable sources of training data.

r002.rationale: It says scalable data and a data-model feedback loop could drive the next big jump, but does not clearly say that this could bring solving robotics within reach.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: how do we give robots enough experience to generalize? We want a robot to work across different tasks, different objects, and different environments. Collecting demonstrations for every possible situation would be very difficult, so we need ways to grow the training data without growing the collection effort at the same rate.

And it’s not just about the amount of data. It’s about diversity and useful feedback. Can the robot learn from an unsuccessful attempt? Can experience on one task help it perform another? Can we use simulation and other sources of experience while making sure those lessons transfer to the physical world?

That’s why I see scalable training data as such an important direction. Better models give us more capacity to learn, but we also need a scalable way to provide the experience those models learn from. The long-term opportunity is to build a cycle where more experience leads to better robots, and better robots can gather more useful experience.

r001.rationale: The response says training data must scale without matching collection effort, but it does not mention teleoperation data or clearly propose replacing it with scalable data.

r002.rationale: It describes a long-term cycle of experience and better robots, but does not say that a breakthrough in scalable training data could bring solving robotics within reach.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the biggest bottlenecks in robotics is still data. In language and vision, you can learn from enormous amounts of text and images on the internet. For robots, we need examples of actions and their consequences—how the world changes when a robot moves or touches something. That kind of data is much harder to collect.

So beyond Gemini Robotics 1.5, an important question is how we can grow the training data without growing the cost of collecting it at the same rate. Collecting every demonstration through human teleoperation is valuable, but it’s difficult to scale that alone. We need ways for robots to collect useful experience, learn from failures, and benefit from simulation and other sources of information.

And it’s not just about quantity. We need diversity: different environments, different objects, and situations that don’t go exactly as expected. That’s what will help robots generalize beyond the tasks we explicitly train them to do. To me, scalable training data is a foundation for making that progress sustainable.

r001.rationale: It says relying on human teleoperation alone is difficult to scale and calls for robots to gather experience and use simulation and other sources to grow training data without proportional collection cost.

r002.rationale: It describes scalable data as a foundation for sustainable progress and generalization, but does not say that a breakthrough could make solving robotics achievable.
